kandidaty.zagolovok: Muru
kandidaty.tekst:
Muru

Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi 20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since.

Muru is his new, AI-assisted Rust server that aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps both in development and production.

As he did with wrapture, he's been publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the project as he works on it - as part of his development process.

Here's everything he's published so far, all in the last three weeks:

- 2026-11-04 — Twenty years of mod_wsgi, and what comes next

- 2026-11-05 — A first look at Muru

- 2026-11-07 — Muru: looking inside the workers

- 2026-11-08 — Muru: how it fits together

- 2026-11-09 — Muru: import once, fork many

- 2026-11-10 — Muru: HTTPS in development

- 2026-11-11 — Muru: WSGI and ASGI together

- 2026-11-11 — AI as a lifestyle choice

- 2026-11-12 — Muru: releases, not restarts

- 2026-11-13 — Muru: canaries without a service mesh

- 2026-11-14 — Muru: a better tenant in a container

- 2026-11-15 — Muru: working with Kubernetes, not around it

- 2026-11-16 — Muru: scaling from what the workers report

- 2026-11-17 — Muru: scaling to zero

- 2026-11-18 — Muru: overlays on a schedule

- 2026-11-19 — Muru: noticing and responding

- 2026-11-20 — Muru: a toolbar on every page

- 2026-11-21 — Muru: tracing in the toolbar

- 2026-11-22 — Muru: when lazy imports help

That post about AI as a lifestyle choice is particularly worth a read:

The AI may be doing a lot of the work on the surface, but deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me, and twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi turns out to be useful for that. I am prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something I would trust, and something you would too.

kandidaty.zagolovok: Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds
kandidaty.tekst: Agent Anomaly Detection now monitors ADK agents running across AWS, Azure, or on-premises by analyzing their traces and logs in your Google Cloud project. By ingesting OpenTelemetry-formatted data through the Telemetry API, it evaluates full conversations for behavioral drift without needing access to the agent's underlying runtime. This enables security teams to detect risks like rogue behaviors, tool misuse, and resource exhaustion across multi-cloud environments.

kandidaty.zagolovok: How to securely connect internal Cloud Run MCP servers to Gemini Enterprise
kandidaty.tekst: How to connect Gemini Enterprise privately to internal StreamableHTTP MCP servers on Cloud Run using Egress Agent Gateway, Private Service Connect, FQDN-scoped Private Cloud DNS, and dual-header OAuth 2.0 authentication.

kandidaty.zagolovok: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies
kandidaty.tekst: Semantic governance policies enable developers to govern AI agents by evaluating every proposed tool call inline before execution. Operating via Agent Gateway, the policy engine checks each action against user intent and plain-language rules to prevent unauthorized data sharing and prompt injection attacks. Developers can easily attach natural-language constraints to their agents and monitor auditable verdicts through Cloud Logging.

kandidaty.zagolovok: How to handle user, connector, and agent auth in Gemini Enterprise with a custom UI
kandidaty.tekst: When building a custom enterprise UI on top of Gemini Enterprise's :streamAssist API, developers must manually implement three core authentication layers. These include authenticating users or workloads via Google Identity or Workforce/Workload Identity Federation, managing third-party 3-legged OAuth (3LO) for Federated Connectors through the Keystore, and configuring on-demand per-tool OAuth for custom ADK agents using Vertex AI Agent Engine and GCP Auth Manager.

kandidaty.tekst:
@gdb: OpenAI models topping the alignment benchmarks:

Цитирует @arena: The Arena Alignment Index has been updated! 

We've refined how our signals detect model failures, providing broader coverage and more reliable judgements. Based on the updated methodology:
- @OpenAI continues to dominate, holding all seven top positions.
- @Anthropic's latest release, Claude Fable 5.2, debuts at #8 with a score of 78.2. Claude Opus 5.5, which ranked #6 on the previous index, is now #17.
- Kimi K3.1 Pro by @Kimi_Moonshot is the biggest upgrade over its predecessor (more info in thread).
- Most open source models are trailing closed releases. The best open model - Kimi K3.1 Pro - occupies #9, and the second best, Mimo-V2.6-Flash, is #26 on the Index, followed by Hy4, Beam, Inkling, DeepSeek and GLM.

The Top-6 lab:
- #1 @OpenAI GPT-6.2 Sol
- #2 @AnthropicAI Claude Fable 5.2
- #3 @Kimi_Moonshot Kimi K3.1 Pro
- #4 @GoogleDeepmind Gemini 4 Hydrogen
- #5 @SpaceXSI Grok 4.7
- #6 @AIatMeta Muse Ember

Alignment Index measures how agents behave in real user sessions across three dimensions:
- Unauthorized Action: Doing what the user didn’t ask for or approve
- Deceptive Completion: Saying work is done, checked or working when it isn't
- False Attribution: Crediting the user with something they never said or did

More insights in the thread🧵

At an average of 6.8 min and $0.98 per generation, GPT-6.2 Astra (high) is the best model for its price point and speed on both Pareto frontiers. Similarly, GPT-6.2 Sol (high) at an average of 4.6 min and $0.22 per generation is on the Preference vs Price and Speed Pareto frontier. GPT-6.2 Sol (high) also offers similar output quality to GPT-6 Astra (max), the former #1 Game Dev model, while being about 4x cheaper and 40% faster.

Congrats to the @OpenAI team on taking the top 3 spots on the leaderboard!
